chapter: Boyhood scene: halls and dance music
title: Barrelhouse pianists, the 'horses' beat and seeing King Oliver in a parade
summary: He names early blues pianists, explains the 'horses' as boogie-woogie, and recalls following his uncles to see King Oliver's band at a funeral parade.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. What did they play? They played piano. All these were piano players? They played the blues, yeah, piano players. Black Nolan, Buckeye Wilford. Yeah, they were always welcome. Shine, regular hunky-tunk piano players. First time I heard what it's called now Boogie Woogie. The first time I heard that beat, my little uncle said, look at that guy playing them horses. He used to call it the horses in New Orleans. It wasn't Boogie Woogie, it was horses, because it sounded like a horse's trotting. That monotonous boogie beat. It sounded like a group of horses trotting. So it kept, it was several in New Orleans called the Boogie, the horses. And which uncle was that? That was Willie. Willie or Lush, neither one. They were two years difference. I was either one or the other. And they were in all kind of mischief. They knew when every band was parading because my grandfather either knew about it, at least downtown. And they were second line and they would take me with them. The first time I heard King Oliver, at a parade at the Central Rock Cemetery, they were coming up St. Claude Street. And we ran down to the Central Rock Cemetery. They had seen this funeral going out that direction. And they knew it would come back up St. Claude Street. That was the true colored section. And we trotted down there 10 or 15 minutes and met them. There was a parade coming back. There was a second line that journey. And we followed them. And while their lupus, they would always stick with the band. They wouldn't be with the second line because they were curious to see who was playing. And I took all the kids idolized the jazz metal. And they were so thrilled when they said, there's King Oliver. I remember King Oliver, tall with his horn. And he was walking slow. And very careful because I think he had a lot of corns or bunions on his feet. It seems as if he was trying to pay more attention to stumping his foot on one of them stones in the street or one of them bricks, half a brick.
